source_text: Illud autem, quod te opponere credidisti vel in isto libro, cui nunc respondeo, vel in his, quos ad Marcellinum scripseras, tunc transisse peccatum, quando omnes homines, ut tuis verbis utar, ille unus fuerunt [n282] , sine difficultate veritas deterit et irrisioni cuiusce prudentis exponit. Nam tali argumento praeter impietatem tuam nihil aliud indicatur, impietatem inquam, qua credis ita esse animarum traducem in Tertulliani olim et Manichaei profanitate damnatam, sicut est etiam corporum tradux, quod tam nefarium est, ut, cum a nobis in ea epistula, quam ad Orientem misimus, vobis fuisset obiectum, tu in his libris, quos nuper ad Bonifacium misisti, negando a te propulsare coneris. Ais enim: Dicunt nos autem animarum traducem confiteri, quod in cuius libris legerint, nescio [n283] , ut a te videlicet nihil dici tale deieres. Porro, ut falsitas tua tuorum verborum collatione prodatur, quomodo traducem animarum, profanam re vera opinionem, tuis dicis sensibus non teneri, cum profitearis omnes homines illum unum fuisse? Si enim non credis partem animae seminibus illigatam, quo ore scribis omnes homines Adam solum fuisse, cum homo utique nisi anima et corpus simul esse non possit?
pass_a_gloss: But that which you believed to oppose either in this book to which I now answer, or in those which you had written to Marcellinus, that sin then passed, when all human beings, to use your words, that one was, the truth wears down without difficulty and exposes to the derision of any prudent person. For by such an argument besides your impiety nothing else is indicated, impiety I say, by which you believe there is a tradux of souls, long ago damned in the profanity of Tertullian and of a Manichaean, just as there is also a tradux of bodies, which is so nefarious that, when it had been objected to you by us in that letter which we sent to the East, you in these books which you recently sent to Boniface try to drive it away from yourself by denying. For you say: But they say that we confess a tradux of souls, which in whose books they have read I do not know, so that namely you may swear that nothing of such a kind is said by you. Further, that your falsehood may be betrayed by a collation of your words, how do you say that a tradux of souls, a truly profane opinion, is not held by your senses, when you profess that all human beings were that one? For if you do not believe a part of the soul bound into seeds, with what mouth do you write that all human beings were Adam alone, when a human being certainly cannot be unless soul and body together?

lemmas.lexica: LS semen; Blaise bodily seed vs transmitted sin
LS tradux=vine-shoot/layer; Blaise tradux peccati=transmission of sin by descent
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
Blaise Manichaeus; Julian's polemic label vs natural evil

pass_b_english: The argument you thought you could oppose to us, whether in the book I am now answering or in those you wrote to Marcellinus, is this: sin passed on at the time when all human beings, to use your own words, ‘were that one man’ (Augustine, Merits and Forgiveness of Sins 1.11). Truth crushes this without difficulty and exposes it to the ridicule of every discerning person. Such an argument reveals nothing except your impiety: the impiety by which you believe in a transmission of souls, long ago condemned in the irreverence of Tertullian and Mani, just as there is a transmission of bodies. This is so abominable that when we charged you with it in the letter we sent to the East, you tried to repel it by denial in the books you recently sent to Boniface. You say: ‘They say, however, that we confess a transmission of souls. In whose books they have read this I do not know’ (Augustine, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians 3.26), thereby swearing that you say nothing of the kind. But to expose your falsehood by comparing your own words: how do you say that transmission of souls—a truly impious opinion—is not held in your understanding, when you profess that all human beings were that one man? If you do not believe a part of the soul is bound into the seed, with what mouth do you write that all human beings were Adam alone, when a human being certainly cannot exist except as soul and body together?

choices.why: Bodily seed of generation; Julian denies it carries a will's sin.
Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
